name: Thread Artist Residency
note: No photo on Commons (no category, no files). Sources confirm the idea (a pitched roof inverted so it drains into two courtyards either side of a central gathering space, workshops and bedrooms at the ends, earth-brick walls, thatch on a steel and bamboo frame) but not the actual roof profile seen from outside, which is the whole point of a drawing. Not drawn; a section from the architect would settle it.

name: Tour Bois-le-Prêtre Transformation
note: No usable photo: Commons has only two files: one blurs the tower (French freedom-of-panorama rules), the other is mostly a street sign in front of the facade. Not drawn because sources disagree on the storey count (16 levels vs R+17, 49-50 m) and none give the tower's footprint or facade width, so the proportions of an elevation would be guessed. Known: 96 flats, prefabricated 7.5 x 3 m winter-garden and balcony modules added to the facades.

name: Yusuhara Wooden Bridge Museum
note: No free photo: the only Kuma photo from Yusuhara on Commons (File:Kumayusuhara.jpg) shows the Kumo-no-ue Hotel, not this museum. Sources confirm the central pier and stacked cedar brackets, but not the shape of the gallery and its 'inverted' roof on top or how the two ends (one 10 m lower) meet the ground, so it is not drawn. The architect sites could not be opened from here.

name: Addis Ababa City Hall
note: No Commons category and no clear photo. File:ET-Addis Abeba, Churchill Road.JPG (CC BY-SA 3.0, 1536x2048) looks up Churchill Avenue and seems to show the City Hall small in the distance, too small for the wall. Sources give 42 m height and a central tower between two wings, but no storey count, wing lengths or facade pattern, so not drawn.

note: No Commons category. The Flickr photo (5184x2912) shows the trellis dome over the plaza. The UAE has no freedom of panorama for buildings, so these files could be challenged on Commons later.

name: Alioune Diop University Teaching and Research Unit
note: No photo on Commons. Sources confirm a long building under a metal double roof that runs out into a 10 m canopy, with a south screen of about 20,000 triangular concrete bricks (an L-shaped screen 'lying on its back') and a 3 m ventilated cavity behind it. None give the number of storeys or the building's length, so the elevation's proportions would be guessed. Not drawn; the Aga Khan Award file has drawings.

name: Aïshti Foundation
note: No photo on Commons (the only 'Aishti' file is a shop display). Sources describe a large, slightly rotated box wrapped in a red aluminium-tube lattice with a zigzag pattern, four floors of art and retail. They don't give its proportions or the pattern's layout, which would be the whole drawing. Not drawn.

name: B018
note: No photo on Commons. Sources agree the club is sunk into the ground under a circular steel lid (like a helipad) whose mirrored plates lift hydraulically at night, but none give how many plates there are, where they hinge or how far they open, which is all a drawing would show. Not drawn.

name: B2 House
note: No photo on Commons. Sources confirm a two-storey concrete and local-stone box on a terrace, east and west ends made of two concrete walls framing a stone wall, the front fully glazed behind reed-filled aluminium shutters. None give its proportions or how many glazed bays/shutters the front has, so not drawn. The AKDN/Archnet award file has drawings if the owner wants it revisited.

name: Bamboo Wing
note: No photo on Commons. Sources describe a bamboo cantilever roof shaped like outstretched wings, about 12 m wide, balancing on one rear leg, built without steel, but not its profile, length or how many column bundles there are. Not drawn.

name: Bee'ah Headquarters
view: side elevation: the tall main dune on the left with its glazed front under the lifted shell edge, a second lower dune behind, both tapering away to the right
note: Commons has one image, File:BEEAH headquarters.jpg (CC BY-SA 4.0 claimed). It is up for deletion since May 2026 (no freedom of panorama in the UAE), and it looks like the architects' render rather than the uploader's own photo, so it isn't safe to use. Sources confirm two linked dunes around a courtyard and a central concrete dome. The profile follows that image; curves are approximate.

name: Beirut Terraces
view: front elevation: a 26-floor tower about 54 m wide and 119.5 m tall, drawn as stacked floor slabs of differing overhang with the glazing set back between them
note: No exterior photo on Commons: the only file in the category shows concrete formwork during construction. Floor count (26), height (119.5 m) and tower width (about 53.7 m) are from sources and set the proportions. The pattern of overhangs is schematic: the real tower repeats five floor types in varying order, so the drawing shows the idea, not each floor's actual depth.
